title: Peter Weyl Theory for General Compact Groups

items.title: The unitary dual of a compact group
items.statement: Let $K$ be a compact Hausdorff topological group. Two strongly continuous unitary representations $\pi,\sigma$ of $K$ are **unitarily equivalent** when there is a unitary intertwiner between them ([[def-strongly-continuous-unitary-representation]]). The **unitary dual** (dual object) $\widehat K$ is the set of unitary equivalence classes of irreducible strongly continuous unitary representations of $K$. By [[thm-continuous-irreducible-unitary-representations-of-compact-groups-are-finite-dimensional]] every class is represented on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space; consequently $\widehat K$ is a set, since every irreducible class admits a representative on $\mathbb C^d$ for some dimension $d\ge1$ ([[def-dimension]], [[cor-finite-dimensional-inner-product-spaces-have-orthonormal-bases]]). When a statement uses a representative $\pi$ of a class or an orthonormal basis of its carrier, such choices are licensed by the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and the assertion must be invariant under unitary equivalence; the same convention is used in [[def-normalized-irreducible-matrix-coefficient-basis]].
items.strategy: Unpack the published notions of unitary representation, irreducible representation and unitary equivalence; use the published finite-dimensionality theorem to bound the carrier dimension of each class, so that classes are realized on the standard spaces $\mathbb C^d$ and form a set. Record the standing AC-based choice of representatives and bases and the invariance obligation; no topology on $\widehat K$ is introduced.

items.title: Representative functions on a compact group
items.statement: Let $K$ be a compact Hausdorff topological group with normalized Haar probability measure $\mu$ ([[cor-normalized-haar-probability-on-a-compact-group]]). A function $f:K\to\mathbb C$ is a **representative function** when there are finitely many finite-dimensional continuous unitary representations $\pi_1,\dots,\pi_r$ of $K$, vectors $v_j,w_j$ in the carrier of $\pi_j$ and scalars $c_j\in\mathbb C$ with $$f=\sum_{j=1}^r c_j\, c^{\pi_j}_{v_j,w_j},\qquad c^{\pi}_{v,w}(k)=\langle\pi(k)v,w\rangle,$$ the matrix coefficient convention of [[def-matrix-coefficient-of-a-unitary-representation]] (linear in $v$, conjugate-linear in $w$). We write $R(K)\subseteq C(K,\mathbb C)$ for the set of representative functions; it is by definition the linear span of the matrix coefficients of continuous finite-dimensional unitary representations of $K$. Since every finite-dimensional continuous representation of $K$ is unitarizable ([[lem-averaging-makes-a-finite-dimensional-representation-unitary]]), $R(K)$ is also the linear span of the matrix coefficients of all continuous finite-dimensional complex representations of $K$.
items.strategy: Unpack the matrix-coefficient definition; coefficients are continuous by [[def-matrix-coefficient-of-a-unitary-representation]]. The unitarization clause transfers the general finite-dimensional case to the unitary one via the published averaging lemma. No completeness, closure or density claim is made here.

items.title: Direct sums and tensor products of finite-dimensional unitary representations
items.statement:
Let $K$ be a topological group and let $\pi_1,\pi_2$ be finite-dimensional continuous unitary representations of $K$ on complex Hilbert spaces $V_1,V_2$, of dimensions $d_1,d_2$.
1. The **direct sum** $\pi_1\oplus\pi_2$ on $V_1\oplus V_2$ is a continuous unitary representation of dimension $d_1+d_2$, and $c^{\pi_1\oplus\pi_2}_{(v_1,v_2),(w_1,w_2)}=c^{\pi_1}_{v_1,w_1}+c^{\pi_2}_{v_2,w_2}$ for all vectors.
2. The **tensor product** $\pi_1\otimes\pi_2$ on the algebraic tensor product $V_1\otimes_{\mathbb C}V_2$ with the action of [[def-tensor-product-of-complex-representations]] carries a unique inner product with $\langle v_1\otimes v_2,w_1\otimes w_2\rangle=\langle v_1,w_1\rangle_{V_1}\langle v_2,w_2\rangle_{V_2}$ on elementary tensors ([[thm-universal-property-of-module-tensor-products]]), making it a finite-dimensional Hilbert space of dimension $d_1d_2$ on which $\pi_1\otimes\pi_2$ is a continuous unitary representation, and $c^{\pi_1\otimes\pi_2}_{v_1\otimes v_2,w_1\otimes w_2}=c^{\pi_1}_{v_1,w_1}\,c^{\pi_2}_{v_2,w_2}$.
3. The trivial one-dimensional representation $1_K$ is a continuous unitary representation with constant matrix coefficient $1$; and for every finite-dimensional continuous unitary $\pi$ on $V$ with an orthonormal basis $e_1,\dots,e_d$, the linear operators defined by $\langle\sigma(k)e_i,e_j\rangle=\overline{\langle\pi(k)e_i,e_j\rangle}$ in that basis form a continuous finite-dimensional unitary representation $\sigma$ of $K$, and $\overline{c^{\pi}_{v,w}}=c^{\sigma}_{Jv,Jw}$ for all $v,w\in V$, where $J(\sum_ia_ie_i)=\sum_i\overline{a_i}e_i$; in particular the conjugate of a matrix coefficient is again such a coefficient.
items.strategy: Direct sums are immediate. For the tensor product choose orthonormal bases of $V_1$ and $V_2$ ([[cor-finite-dimensional-inner-product-spaces-have-orthonormal-bases]]) and define the inner product on the basis $e_i\otimes f_j$ by declaring it orthonormal; then verify the displayed elementary-tensor formula by sesquilinearity and positive-definiteness by expansion, and identify the two descriptions of the inner product. Unitarity and continuity follow because all matrix entries of $\pi_1\otimes\pi_2$ are products of continuous matrix entries of $\pi_1$ and $\pi_2$; the conjugation identity is the conjugate symmetry of the inner product. These standard operations are what make the representative functions an algebra.

items.title: Representative functions form a self-adjoint translation-invariant algebra
items.statement: Let $K$ be a compact Hausdorff topological group. The set $R(K)$ of representative functions ([[def-representative-function-on-a-compact-group]]) contains every constant function and is closed under pointwise addition, pointwise multiplication, complex conjugation, and left and right translation: for $f\in R(K)$ and $g\in K$ the functions $k\mapsto f(g^{-1}k)$ and $k\mapsto f(kg)$ again lie in $R(K)$. In particular $R(K)$ is a self-adjoint unital complex function algebra on $K$ ([[def-self-adjoint-complex-function-algebra]]).
items.strategy: Sums and scalar multiples are part of the definition; constants come from $1_K$; products and conjugates are the elementary-tensor and swapped-argument identities of [[lem-direct-sums-and-tensor-products-of-finite-dimensional-unitary-representations]]. For translations use unitarity: if $f=c^{\pi}_{v,w}$, then the functions $k\mapsto f(g^{-1}k)$ and $k\mapsto f(kg)$ equal $c^{\pi}_{v,\pi(g)w}$ and $c^{\pi}_{\pi(g)v,w}$, both coefficients of the same finite-dimensional unitary representation. This proves the algebra and self-adjointness axioms; point separation is deliberately not claimed here.

items.title: Compact convolution operators commute with right translations and have conjugate-kernel adjoints
items.statement:
Let $K$ be a compact Hausdorff group with normalized Haar probability $\mu$, let $\varphi\in L^2(K,\mu;\mathbb C)$ and let $C_\varphi$ be left convolution by $\varphi$ on $L^2(K)$, $(C_\varphi h)(x)=\int_K\varphi(xy^{-1})h(y)\,d\mu(y)$ ([[lem-compact-convolution-operators-are-hilbert-schmidt]]).
1. For every $g\in K$, $C_\varphi\rho(g)=\rho(g)C_\varphi$, where $\rho(g)h(x)=h(xg)$ is the right regular unitary representation ([[def-left-and-right-regular-unitary-representations]]); here $\Delta_K\equiv1$ because compact groups are unimodular ([[prop-compact-discrete-and-abelian-groups-are-unimodular]]).
2. With $\varphi^*(k):=\overline{\varphi(k^{-1})}$ one has $C_\varphi^*=C_{\varphi^*}$; hence if $\varphi^*=\varphi$ almost everywhere then $C_\varphi$ is self-adjoint. Moreover, when $\varphi=\varphi^*$, every eigenspace $\ker(C_\varphi-\lambda I)$ for $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ (the case $\lambda=0$ being the kernel $\ker C_\varphi$) is $\rho(K)$-invariant.
items.strategy: For (1) change variables in the defining integral using right invariance of $\mu$ and the identity $xg\,y^{-1}=x(gy)^{-1}$. For (2) use the Hilbert-adjoint characterization and inversion invariance of Haar measure: $\langle C_\varphi h_1,h_2\rangle=\int\int\varphi(xy^{-1})h_1(y)\overline{h_2(x)}\,d\mu(y)d\mu(x)$ and the substitution $y\mapsto y^{-1}$, $x\mapsto x^{-1}$ produces $C_{\varphi^*}$. Fubini for $L^1$ functions on the finite measure space $K\times K$ justifies the interchange ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]). Invariance of kernels is immediate from (1) and bounded-operator uniqueness of adjoints. AC is used through the normalized Haar probability and the published L2 and adjoint suppliers; the commutation computation itself is choice-free apart from those inputs.

items.title: Finite-rank spectral pieces of a self-adjoint compact convolution operator
items.statement:
Let $K$ be a compact Hausdorff group with normalized Haar probability $\mu$ and let $\varphi\in L^2(K,\mu;\mathbb C)$ satisfy $\varphi^*=\varphi$ (so $C_\varphi$ is compact and self-adjoint, [[lem-compact-convolution-operators-commute-with-right-translations]], [[lem-compact-convolution-operators-are-hilbert-schmidt]]). Let $\Sigma=\{\lambda\ne0:\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue of }C_\varphi\}$ and $E_\lambda=\ker(C_\varphi-\lambda I)$.
1. $\Sigma$ is finite or countably infinite, each $E_\lambda$ is finite dimensional, distinct eigenspaces are orthogonal, and the closed linear span of $\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Sigma}E_\lambda$ is $(\ker C_\varphi)^\perp$, so $L^2(K)=\ker C_\varphi\oplus\widehat\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Sigma}E_\lambda$ is an orthogonal Hilbert-space direct sum.
2. Every $E_\lambda$ ($\lambda\in\Sigma$) and $\ker C_\varphi$ are invariant under the right regular representation $\rho$; consequently each $E_\lambda$ is a finite-dimensional continuous unitary representation of $K$ under $\rho$.
items.strategy: Apply the published spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators, which gives finite multiplicities, orthogonality, the description of the closed span of the nonzero eigenspaces as $(\ker T)^\perp$, and the eigenbasis corollary. Invariance is from [[lem-compact-convolution-operators-commute-with-right-translations]]: a bounded operator commuting with $C_\varphi$ preserves every eigenspace and the kernel. Strong continuity and unitarity of the restricted action are inherited from the right regular representation (published), and finite dimension makes the representation continuous in the finite-dimensional sense. The spectral-theorem and eigenbasis suppliers assume Countable Choice, hence AC; the item declares AC for that use.

items.title: Matrix coefficients of finite-dimensional representations separate points of a compact group
items.statement: Let $K$ be a compact Hausdorff group with normalized Haar probability $\mu$. For all distinct $x,y\in K$ there exist a finite-dimensional continuous unitary representation $\pi$ of $K$ and vectors $v,w$ in its carrier with $\langle\pi(x)v,w\rangle\ne\langle\pi(y)v,w\rangle$. Equivalently, the finite-dimensional continuous unitary representations of $K$ separate the points of $K$.

items.title: Uniform density of representative functions (topological Peter-Weyl theorem)
items.statement: Let $K$ be a compact Hausdorff topological group. The representative functions $R(K)$ are uniformly dense in $C(K,\mathbb C)$: for every $f\in C(K,\mathbb C)$ and every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $h\in R(K)$ with $\sup_{k\in K}|f(k)-h(k)|<\varepsilon$.
items.strategy: By [[lem-representative-functions-form-a-self-adjoint-translation-invariant-algebra]], $R(K)$ is a unital self-adjoint complex function algebra on the compact Hausdorff space $K$, and by [[lem-compact-group-matrix-coefficients-separate-points]] it separates points. The unital case of the published complex Stone-Weierstrass theorem ([[thm-complex-stone-weierstrass-self-adjoint]], [[def-self-adjoint-complex-function-algebra]]) applies verbatim and yields uniform density. This is the topological form of Peter-Weyl and is the only density statement used downstream.

items.title: The normalized irreducible matrix coefficient family
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a compact Hausdorff group with normalized Haar probability $\mu$ and unitary dual $\widehat K$ ([[def-unitary-dual-of-a-compact-group]]). For each class $\pi\in\widehat K$ fix a representative, still written $\pi$, on a finite-dimensional carrier $H_\pi$ with $d_\pi:=\dim_{\mathbb C}H_\pi\ge1$ ([[thm-continuous-irreducible-unitary-representations-of-compact-groups-are-finite-dimensional]]), and fix an orthonormal basis $e^\pi_1,\dots,e^\pi_{d_\pi}$ ([[cor-finite-dimensional-inner-product-spaces-have-orthonormal-bases]]); both choices are licensed by AC. The **normalized irreducible matrix coefficient family** is $$\mathcal B=\bigl(u^\pi_{ij}\bigr)_{\pi\in\widehat K,\ 1\le i,j\le d_\pi},\qquad u^\pi_{ij}(k):=\sqrt{d_\pi}\,\langle\pi(k)e^\pi_i,e^\pi_j\rangle .$$ Different choices of representatives and orthonormal bases produce the same family up to relabeling of indices and a unitary change of coordinates in each block; the normalization $\sqrt{d_\pi}$ is fixed precisely so that Schur orthogonality ([[thm-schur-orthogonality-for-compact-groups]], part 2 with its $1/d$ constant in the convention $\langle\pi(k)v,w\rangle$) makes the family orthonormal.
items.strategy: Define the family from the published matrix-coefficient and orthogonality items, record the AC use for representatives and bases, and verify the stated choice-invariance: a change of orthonormal basis acts by a unitary $U$, sending $u^\pi_{ij}$ to the corresponding block entries multiplied by $U$ on the appropriate side. No completeness claim is made here; it is [[thm-l2-peter-weyl-orthonormal-basis]].

items.title: The normalized matrix coefficients form an orthonormal basis of L2(K)
items.statement: Let $K$ be a compact Hausdorff group with normalized Haar probability $\mu$ and let $\mathcal B=(u^\pi_{ij})$ be the normalized irreducible matrix coefficient family ([[def-normalized-irreducible-matrix-coefficient-basis]]). Then $\mathcal B$ is an orthonormal family in $L^2(K,\mu;\mathbb C)$ and its closed linear span is all of $L^2(K)$; equivalently, $\mathcal B$ is an orthonormal basis (Hilbert basis) of $L^2(K)$, and $\sum_{\pi,i,j}|\langle f,u^\pi_{ij}\rangle|^2=\|f\|_2^2$ for every $f\in L^2(K)$.
items.strategy: Orthonormality: for classes $\pi\ne\sigma$ the inner product of any two coefficients vanishes by the inequivalent-pair part of Schur orthogonality, while for the same $\pi$ the stated $1/d_\pi$ normalization and the orthonormal bases give $\langle u^\pi_{ij},u^\pi_{kl}\rangle=\delta_{ik}\delta_{jl}$. Completeness: every matrix coefficient of every finite-dimensional continuous unitary representation is a finite linear combination of the $u^\pi_{ij}$: by complete reducibility ([[thm-finite-dimensional-compact-group-representations-are-completely-reducible]]) the representation is a finite direct sum of irreducibles, coefficients split over direct sums, and within an irreducible the chosen orthonormal basis expands the coefficient. Hence the span of $\mathcal B$ contains $R(K)$; by [[thm-uniform-peter-weyl-density]] that span is uniformly dense in $C(K)$, and $C(K)$ is dense in $L^2(K)$ ([[lem-complex-haar-l1-and-l2-are-complete-and-cc-dense]]), so the closed span of $\mathcal B$ is $L^2(K)$. The published Parseval equivalences for complete orthonormal families turn this into the stated identity and the basis property.

items.title: Hilbert direct sums of unitary representations
items.statement: Let $I$ be a set and let $(H_i)_{i\in I}$ be complex Hilbert spaces. The **Hilbert direct sum** $\widehat\bigoplus_{i\in I}H_i$ is the set of families $v=(v_i)_{i\in I}$ with $v_i\in H_i$ and $\sum_{i\in I}\|v_i\|^2<\infty$ in the finite-subset-supremum convention ([[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]), with componentwise linear structure and inner product $\langle v,w\rangle=\sum_{i\in I}\langle v_i,w_i\rangle$; it is a complex Hilbert space, and the canonical maps $H_i\to\widehat\bigoplus_jH_j$ (extend by zero) are linear isometries with pairwise orthogonal closed images whose closed linear span is the whole space ([[thm-hilbert-space-with-a-given-orthonormal-basis-is-ell-two-of-the-index-set]], [[lem-square-summable-orthogonal-families-have-norm-convergent-finite-sums]]). If each $H_i$ carries a strongly continuous unitary representation $\pi_i$ of a topological group $K$, the **Hilbert direct sum of the representations**, still written $\widehat\bigoplus_i\pi_i$, is the componentwise action; it is again a strongly continuous unitary representation. A strongly continuous unitary representation $\pi$ of $K$ on $H$ is the **Hilbert direct sum of a family of subrepresentations** $(H_i,\pi_i)$ when the $H_i$ are pairwise orthogonal closed $\pi(K)$-invariant subspaces of $H$ with closed linear span $H$ and $\pi|_{H_i}=\pi_i$; equivalently the canonical map $\widehat\bigoplus_iH_i\to H$, $(v_i)\mapsto\sum_iv_i$, is a unitary intertwiner.
items.strategy: Build the space from the published $\ell^2$ model of a Hilbert space with an orthonormal basis, verifying the inner product and the orthogonal isometric embeddings. Strong continuity of the componentwise action: given $v$ and $\varepsilon$, choose a finite set $F$ carrying all but $\varepsilon/3$ of the square sum, use continuity of the finitely many $\pi_i$, and control the tail by square summability; unitarity is componentwise. The subrepresentation form is the canonical isometry statement, with invariance giving intertwining.

items.title: The L1 action of a strongly continuous unitary representation
items.strategy: Bochner integrability follows from strong measurability of $k\mapsto\pi(k)v$, continuity on the compact group, and $\int|f|\,\|v\|<\infty$ ([[thm-bochner-integrability-criterion]]); the norm inequality is [[lem-bochner-integral-norm-inequality]]. Multiplicativity and adjointness use Fubini, Haar invariance and inversion invariance ([[thm-integrals-are-invariant-under-measure-preserving-maps]]); the covariance identities are change-of-variables identities for the L1 convolution conventions ([[def-convolution-on-cc-and-l1-of-a-group]]). For (3) evaluate the Bochner integral of $f(k)(\pi(k)v-v)$; uniform continuity of $k\mapsto\pi(k)v$ on compact $K$ lets a nonnegative continuous $f$ of total mass one and small support satisfy $\|\pi(f)v-v\|<\|v\|$, so $\pi(f)v\ne0$ ([[lem-lch-urysohn-cutoff-for-a-compact-set-inside-an-open-set]]).

items.title: Every nonzero unitary representation of a compact group has a finite-dimensional subrepresentation
items.statement: Let $K$ be a compact Hausdorff group and let $\pi:K\to U(H)$ be a strongly continuous unitary representation on a complex Hilbert space $H\ne\{0\}$. Then $H$ contains a nonzero finite-dimensional closed $\pi(K)$-invariant subspace.
items.strategy:
Fix $v
e0$. By [[lem-l1-action-of-a-unitary-representation]] choose $f\in C(K)$ with $\pi(f)v
e0$. By [[thm-uniform-peter-weyl-density]] approximate $f$ uniformly, hence in $L^1$ since $\mu(K)=1$, by a finite linear combination $f_1\in R(K)$ of matrix coefficients; then $\|\pi(f)v-\pi(f_1)v\|\le\|f-f_1\|_1\|v\|$, so for a close enough $f_1$ we have $\pi(f_1)v
e0$. Let $E\subseteq C(K)$ be the finite-dimensional space of matrix coefficients of the finitely many finite-dimensional representations occurring in $f_1$; it is invariant under left translation ([[lem-representative-functions-form-a-self-adjoint-translation-invariant-algebra]]) and finite dimensional. Then $F:=\{\pi(h)v:h\in E\}$ is a finite-dimensional vector space containing $\pi(f_1)v
e0$, and the covariance identity of [[lem-l1-action-of-a-unitary-representation]] gives $\pi(k)\pi(h)v=\pi(\lambda(k)h)v\in F$ for all $k\in K,h\in E$. Hence the closure of the finite-dimensional space $F$ is a nonzero finite-dimensional closed invariant subspace. AC enters only through the L1 action and the uniform density supplier; the finite-dimensionality argument itself is choice-free apart from those inputs.

items.title: Peter-Weyl decomposition of the regular representation
items.statement:
Let $K$ be a compact Hausdorff group with normalized Haar probability $\mu$ and let $\lambda,\rho$ be the left and right regular unitary representations of $K$ on $L^2(K,\mu;\mathbb C)$ ([[def-left-and-right-regular-unitary-representations]]; $K$ is unimodular so $\Delta_K\equiv1$). For $\pi\in\widehat K$ let $M_\pi\subseteq C(K)$ be the span of all matrix coefficients of $\pi$. Then:
1. $M_\pi$ is finite dimensional of dimension $d_\pi^2$ and is the closed span of the block $\{u^\pi_{ij}\}_{i,j}$ of [[def-normalized-irreducible-matrix-coefficient-basis]]; distinct $M_\pi,M_\sigma$ are orthogonal, and $L^2(K)=\widehat\bigoplus_{\pi\in\widehat K}M_\pi$ ([[def-hilbert-direct-sum-of-unitary-representations]]).
2. The linear isomorphism $H_\pi\otimes\overline{H_\pi}\to M_\pi$, $v\otimes\overline w\mapsto c^\pi_{v,w}$, intertwines the $K\times K$-structure: $\rho(g)$ acts on the $H_\pi$ factor by $\pi(g)$ and $\lambda(g)$ acts on the conjugate factor $\overline{H_\pi}$ by the conjugate representation $\overline\pi(g)$. Consequently $\rho|_{M_\pi}\cong d_\pi\,\pi$ and $\lambda|_{M_\pi}\cong d_\pi\,\overline\pi$.
3. Hence $\rho\cong\widehat\bigoplus_{\pi\in\widehat K}d_\pi\,\pi$ and $\lambda\cong\widehat\bigoplus_{\pi\in\widehat K}d_\pi\,\overline\pi$; since $\pi\mapsto\overline\pi$ is a bijection of $\widehat K$ with $d_{\overline\pi}=d_\pi$, also $\lambda\cong\widehat\bigoplus_{\pi\in\widehat K}d_\pi\,\pi$, so the left regular representation is the Hilbert direct sum of $d_\pi$ copies of $\pi$ and the right regular representation acts on the dual factor of each coefficient block.
items.strategy: The block $M_\pi$ is finite dimensional because it is spanned by the $d_\pi^2$ functions $u^\pi_{ij}$, and the two-sided translation computations $\rho(g)u^\pi_{ij}=\sum_l\langle\pi(g)e_i,e_l\rangle u^\pi_{lj}$, $\lambda(g)u^\pi_{ij}=\sum_l\overline{\langle\pi(g)e_j,e_l\rangle}u^\pi_{il}$ exhibit the first-factor $\pi$ action and the second-factor conjugate action; the tensor identification follows by writing $c^\pi_{v,w}$ in the orthonormal bases. Orthogonality of distinct blocks and the Hilbert direct sum are [[thm-l2-peter-weyl-orthonormal-basis]]. Reindexing the orthogonal sum by $\pi\mapsto\overline\pi$ gives the final form. AC is used for the normalized Haar probability and for the published regular-representation and Schur-orthogonality suppliers.

items.title: Unitary representations of compact groups are discrete Hilbert sums of irreducibles
items.strategy: (i) A nonzero unitary representation contains a nonzero finite-dimensional subrepresentation by [[lem-a-nonzero-unitary-representation-of-a-compact-group-has-a-finite-dimensional-subrepresentation]], which by complete reducibility of finite-dimensional compact-group representations ([[thm-finite-dimensional-compact-group-representations-are-completely-reducible]]) contains an irreducible one; (ii) order by extension the families of pairwise orthogonal finite-dimensional irreducible subrepresentations and apply Zorn ([[thm-zorn]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]); the upper bound of a chain is the closed span of its union, which is a Hilbert direct sum of the chain's pieces; (iii) maximality forces the closed span to be $H$, since otherwise the orthogonal complement is a nonzero invariant subspace and (i) produces a new irreducible summand, contradicting maximality; (iv) grouping the irreducible summands by unitary-equivalence class exhibits $H=\widehat\bigoplus_\sigma H_{(\sigma)}$ and identifies $H_{(\sigma)}$ with the range of $P_\sigma$ using the published isotypic projection properties; (v) finite-dimensionality of irreducibles is the published theorem. Invariance, orthogonality and the Hilbert-sum structure are maintained at every step.

items.title: Parseval and Fourier inversion for compact groups
items.statement:
Let $K$ be a compact Hausdorff group with normalized Haar probability $\mu$, with normalized matrix coefficient family $\mathcal B=(u^\pi_{ij})$ ([[def-normalized-irreducible-matrix-coefficient-basis]]). For $f\in L^2(K)$ and each $\pi\in\widehat K$ put $\pi(f):=\int_Kf(k)\pi(k)^{-1}\,d\mu(k)\in\operatorname{End}(H_\pi)$ (the L1 action of [[lem-l1-action-of-a-unitary-representation]] applied to the reflected representative).
1. **Parseval/Plancherel.** For every $f\in L^2(K)$, $$\sum_{\pi\in\widehat K}\ \sum_{i,j=1}^{d_\pi}\bigl|\langle f,u^\pi_{ij}\rangle\bigr|^2=\|f\|_2^2,\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \sum_{\pi\in\widehat K}d_\pi\,\|\pi(f)\|_{HS}^2=\|f\|_2^2,$$ where $\|\cdot\|_{HS}$ is the Hilbert-Schmidt norm ([[def-hilbert-schmidt-operator]]).
2. **Fourier inversion in $L^2$.** The finite-subset net of spectral partial sums $\sum_{\pi,i,j}\langle f,u^\pi_{ij}\rangle\,u^\pi_{ij}$ converges to $f$ in $L^2(K)$.
3. **Exactness on the coefficient algebra.** If $f\in R(K)$ is a finite linear combination of the $u^\pi_{ij}$, its expansion is that finite sum and equals $f$ pointwise; in particular no uniform convergence of partial sums is asserted for arbitrary continuous $f$.
items.strategy: Part 1 is the Parseval identity of [[thm-l2-peter-weyl-orthonormal-basis]] together with the identity $|\langle f,u^\pi_{ij}\rangle|^2=d_\pi\,|(\pi(f))_{ij}|^2$, which follows from the definition of $u^\pi_{ij}$ and Schur orthogonality. Part 2 is the net convergence of the expansion in a complete orthonormal family. Part 3 is immediate from finite linearity. No pointwise or uniform inversion is claimed outside the coefficient algebra; uniform approximation of general continuous functions is the separate density theorem [[thm-uniform-peter-weyl-density]]. AC is inherited through the L1 action and the orthonormal-basis theorem; the corollary adds no independent choice.

items.title: Each vector has at most countably many nonzero isotypic components
items.statement: Let $K$ be a compact Hausdorff group and let $\pi$ be a strongly continuous unitary representation of $K$ on a complex Hilbert space $H$, with isotypic decomposition $H=\widehat\bigoplus_{\sigma\in\widehat K}H_{(\sigma)}$ ([[thm-arbitrary-unitary-representations-of-compact-groups-decompose-discretely]]). For every $v\in H$ the set $\{\sigma\in\widehat K:v_{(\sigma)}\ne0\}$ of classes whose isotypic component meets $v$ nontrivially is at most countable, where $v_{(\sigma)}$ is the orthogonal projection of $v$ to $H_{(\sigma)}$. In particular each single $f\in L^2(K)$ has nonzero components in at most countably many isotypic summands of the Peter-Weyl decomposition ([[thm-regular-representation-peter-weyl-decomposition]]). No countability of $\widehat K$ and no countability of a Hilbert basis of $H$ is asserted.
items.strategy: The Hilbert direct sum gives $\sum_{\sigma}\|v_{(\sigma)}\|^2=\|v\|^2<\infty$ in the finite-subset-supremum convention. For each $n\ge1$ the set $F_n=\{\sigma:\|v_{(\sigma)}\|>1/n\}$ is finite, because any finite subset of it contributes more than $|F|/n$ to the total sum. Hence the support is the countable union $\bigcup_nF_n$ of finite sets, so at most countable. The regular-representation instance is the special case $H=L^2(K)$. No countability of the dual or of a basis is claimed. AC is inherited through the decomposition theorem; the support-counting argument itself is choice-free.

items.title: Continuous finite-dimensional representations of profinite groups factor through finite quotients
items.statement: Let $K$ be a profinite group ([[def-profinite-group-by-inverse-limit]]) and let $\rho:K\to U(n)$ be a continuous homomorphism, regarded as a continuous finite-dimensional unitary representation on $\mathbb C^n$ ([[def-strongly-continuous-unitary-representation]]). Then $\ker\rho$ is open in $K$, and $\rho$ factors through the finite quotient $K/\ker\rho$: there are a finite group $F$, a surjective continuous homomorphism $q:K\to F$ and a homomorphism $\bar\rho:F\to U(n)$ with $\rho=\bar\rho\circ q$. More precisely, if $K=\varprojlim_iG_i$ with coordinate projections $\pi_i$, then $\ker\pi_i\subseteq\ker\rho$ for some $i$, so $\rho$ factors through the finite quotient $K/\ker\pi_i$ of $K$ (isomorphic to the image $\pi_i(K)$, a subgroup of the finite group $G_i$). Consequently every matrix coefficient of $\rho$ is locally constant on $K$ and factors through a finite quotient.
items.strategy: Regard $U(n)$ as a finite-dimensional Lie group ([[ex-unitary-and-special-unitary-lie-groups]], [[def-lie-group]]) and apply no small subgroups ([[lem-no-small-subgroups-in-a-lie-group]]): there is an identity neighbourhood $V\subseteq U(n)$ containing no subgroup other than $\{e\}$. Then $\rho^{-1}(V)$ is an identity neighbourhood in $K$. The kernels $\ker\pi_i$ form an open normal neighbourhood basis at the identity ([[lem-kernels-of-finite-projections-form-an-open-normal-neighbourhood-basis]]), so $\ker\pi_i\subseteq\rho^{-1}(V)$ for some $i$. Then $\rho(\ker\pi_i)\subseteq V$ is a subgroup of $V$, hence trivial, so $\ker\pi_i\subseteq\ker\rho$; therefore $\ker\rho$ is open. The quotient $K/\ker\rho$ is discrete (quotient by an open subgroup) and compact (continuous image of the compact group $K$), hence finite, and the first isomorphism theorem for groups provides the factorization ([[thm-first-isomorphism-theorem-groups]], [[def-quotient-topology]], [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]). AC supplies the countable choice assumed by the published U(n) Lie-group example; the no-small-subgroups and neighbourhood-basis arguments are choice-free.

items.title: Peter-Weyl for a profinite group
items.statement: Let $K$ be a profinite group ([[def-profinite-group-by-inverse-limit]]), with its normalized Haar probability $\mu$ ([[cor-normalized-haar-probability-on-a-compact-group]]); $K$ is compact, Hausdorff and totally disconnected, and is a genuinely non-Lie compact group unless it is finite. Every continuous finite-dimensional unitary representation of $K$ factors through a finite quotient $K/N$, $N$ open normal ([[lem-continuous-finite-dimensional-representations-of-profinite-groups-factor-through-finite-quotients]]). For such a representation $\pi=\bar\pi\circ q$ with $q:K\to F=K/N$ finite, the linear map $v\otimes\overline w\mapsto(k\mapsto\langle\bar\pi(q(k))v,w\rangle)$ identifies the coefficient space of $\pi$ with the pullback to $K$ of the coefficient space of the finite-dimensional representation $\bar\pi$ of the finite group $F$; in particular the coefficient space is finite dimensional of dimension $(\dim\pi)^2$ and consists of locally constant functions constant on the cosets of $N$. The unitary dual of $K$ is exactly the set of classes of pullbacks of irreducible representations of the finite quotients $K/N$ ($N$ open normal), and $R(K)$ is the union, over such $N$, of the pullbacks of $R(K/N)$; since each $K/N$ is finite, $R(K)$ consists exactly of the locally constant functions and is uniformly dense in $C(K)$ by [[thm-uniform-peter-weyl-density]], while the normalized coefficient family of [[thm-l2-peter-weyl-orthonormal-basis]] is an orthonormal basis of $L^2(K)$. Thus Peter-Weyl theory applies verbatim to profinite groups such as Galois groups of infinite algebraic extensions and $\mathbb Z_p$-adic groups, whose duals can be extremely complicated but whose harmonic analysis is governed by the same theorem.
items.strategy: Use the factorization lemma to replace every continuous finite-dimensional representation by one of a finite quotient, then compute the coefficient space as the pullback of the finite group's coefficient space (finite dimensional, locally constant). Irreducibility is preserved and reflected under pullback along the surjection $K\to F$; conversely every representation of a finite quotient pulls back to $K$. Density and the orthonormal-basis statement are the general theorems of the A page, which apply because $K$ is compact Hausdorff. No countability or classification of the dual is asserted.

items.title: Continuous finite-dimensional representations of a product of finite groups factor through a finite subproduct
items.statement: Let $(G_i)_{i\in I}$ be finite discrete groups, let $K:=\prod_{i\in I}G_i$ carry the product topology, and for a finite $F\subseteq I$ let $p_F:K\to K_F:=\prod_{i\in F}G_i$ be the coordinate projection. Then $K$ is a profinite group (it is the inverse limit of the finite groups $K_F$ over the directed set of finite subsets $F\subseteq I$), and for every continuous finite-dimensional unitary representation $\rho$ of $K$ there is a finite $F\subseteq I$ and a representation $\rho_F$ of the finite group $K_F$ with $\rho=\rho_F\circ p_F$. Moreover the open normal subgroup $\ker p_F=\prod_{i\notin F}G_i$ can be chosen inside any prescribed identity neighbourhood, and every matrix coefficient of $\rho$ depends on the coordinates in $F$ only.
items.strategy: Present $K$ as the inverse limit of the finite products $K_F$ ([[def-compatible-tuple-inverse-limit-of-groups]], [[def-inverse-limit-topology-for-finite-discrete-groups]], [[thm-concrete-inverse-limit-universal-property-in-groups]]); hence $K$ is profinite ([[def-profinite-group-by-inverse-limit]]) and the kernels $\ker p_F$ form an open normal neighbourhood basis at the identity ([[lem-kernels-of-finite-projections-form-an-open-normal-neighbourhood-basis]]). Apply [[lem-continuous-finite-dimensional-representations-of-profinite-groups-factor-through-finite-quotients]] to obtain an open normal $N\subseteq\rho^{-1}(V)$ with $\rho$ trivial on $N$; choosing a basic identity neighbourhood $\ker p_F=\prod_{i\notin F}G_i$ inside $N$ (product topology, [[def-product-topology]]) gives the factorization through $K_F=K/\ker p_F$; matrix coefficients are then functions of the coordinates in $F$ ([[thm-first-isomorphism-theorem-groups]]).

items.title: Peter-Weyl for an infinite product of finite groups
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $(G_i)_{i\in I}$ be finite discrete groups with $I$ arbitrary and let $K:=\prod_{i\in I}G_i$ with the product topology; $K$ is compact, Hausdorff and totally disconnected, hence profinite with normalized Haar probability $\mu$. By [[lem-continuous-finite-dimensional-representations-of-a-product-of-finite-groups-factor-through-a-finite-subproduct]], every continuous finite-dimensional unitary representation of $K$ factors through the projection $p_F:K\to K_F=\prod_{i\in F}G_i$ for some finite $F\subseteq I$; conversely every finite-dimensional representation of the finite group $K_F$ pulls back to $K$, and it is irreducible exactly when the representation of $K_F$ is irreducible (pullback along the surjection $p_F$). The finite-coordinate irreducibles of $K$ are therefore exactly the pullbacks of the irreducibles of the finite groups $K_F$; their coefficient spaces are the pullbacks of the coefficient spaces of $K_F$, and the coefficient algebra $R(K)$ is the union of these pullbacks over finite $F$, i.e. the algebra of continuous functions depending on finitely many coordinates. This algebra is dense in $C(K)$ by [[thm-uniform-peter-weyl-density]] (equivalently by Stone-Weierstrass: it is a unital self-adjoint algebra separating points because coordinates separate points and the finite-group coefficient algebra separates points), the normalized coefficient family is an orthonormal basis of $L^2(K)$ ([[thm-l2-peter-weyl-orthonormal-basis]]), and the regular representation decomposes as in [[thm-regular-representation-peter-weyl-decomposition]]. No countability of $I$ or of the dual is assumed, and point separation in the product uses only finitely many coordinates.
items.strategy: Present $K$ as the inverse limit of the finite products $K_F$ and apply the factorization lemma; pullback along the surjection preserves and reflects irreducibility. Identify the coefficient algebra with the union of the finite-coordinate pullbacks and invoke the general density and orthonormal-basis theorems. For the direct Stone-Weierstrass alternative, verify the algebra is unital, self-adjoint, and separating: two distinct points differ in some coordinate, and within the resulting finite product the finite-dimensional representation theory separates points. No countability of the dual is claimed.

items.title: The circle: the Peter-Weyl basis is the integer characters
items.strategy: For (1), an irreducible unitary representation of an abelian group has every $\pi(g)$ in the commutant, hence scalar by Schur's lemma, so every one-dimensional subspace is invariant and irreducibility forces dimension one; the coefficient of a one-dimensional unitary representation is its character. For (2) use the published orthonormality and completeness of the trigonometric system. For (3) note that each $z^n$ is a normalized coefficient (degree one, $u^n_{11}=z^n$) so $\{z^n\}\subseteq\mathcal B$; a complete orthonormal subfamily of an orthonormal basis must equal it, since a vector of the basis outside the subfamily would be orthogonal to the subfamily's closed span, which is the whole space. This identifies the dual and the decomposition without a separate computation of $\operatorname{Hom}_{cts}(\mathbb T,\mathbb T)$. AC is inherited through the basis theorem and Schur's lemma; no separate choice is made in the example.

items.title: An L1 function whose modulus is invariant under all translations of the line is zero
items.statement: Let $g\in L^1(\mathbb R,\lambda_1)$ and suppose that for every $t\in\mathbb R$ one has $g(x-t)=g(x)$ for almost every $x\in\mathbb R$. Then $g=0$ almost everywhere. Consequently, if $v\in L^2(\mathbb R,\lambda_1)$ satisfies $|v(x-t)|=|v(x)|$ for every $t\in\mathbb R$ and almost every $x$, then $v=0$ almost everywhere (apply the first statement to $g=|v|^2\in L^1$).
items.strategy: Take identity neighbourhoods $U_n=(-1/n,1/n)$ and functions $e_n\in C_c(\mathbb R)$, $e_n\ge0$, $\operatorname{supp}e_n\subseteq U_n$, $\|e_n\|_1=1$, which exist by the published approximate identity theorem for $L^1$ of a locally compact group applied to the additive group $\mathbb R$ ([[thm-l1-group-algebras-have-a-contractively-bounded-approximate-identity]], [[ex-lebesgue-measure-as-haar-measure-on-rn]]). For each fixed $t$ and almost every $x$, translation invariance with shift $t$ gives $g(t-x)=g(-x)$; hence $(g*e_n)(t)=\int g(t-x)e_n(x)\,dx=\int g(-x)e_n(x)\,dx$ is independent of $t$, so $g*e_n$ is constant. Since $\|g*e_n-g\|_1\to0$, a subsequence converges to $g$ almost everywhere ([[cor-l-one-convergence-has-an-almost-everywhere-convergent-subsequence]]), so $g$ agrees a.e. with a constant; a nonzero constant is not in $L^1(\mathbb R)$, so the constant is $0$.

items.title: The regular representation of R is not a Hilbert direct sum of irreducibles
items.statement:
**Statement refuted.** The compact-group Peter-Weyl conclusion — that every continuous unitary representation of a compact group is a Hilbert direct sum of finite-dimensional irreducible unitary subrepresentations — extends to every locally compact group; in particular the left regular representation of $\mathbb R$ on $L^2(\mathbb R,\lambda_1)$ is a Hilbert direct sum of finite-dimensional irreducible unitary subrepresentations.
**Counterexample.** Let $\lambda$ be the left regular representation of the additive group $\mathbb R$ on $L^2(\mathbb R,\lambda_1)$ ([[def-left-and-right-regular-unitary-representations]], [[thm-regular-representations-are-unitary-and-strongly-continuous]], [[ex-lebesgue-measure-as-haar-measure-on-rn]], [[prop-compact-discrete-and-abelian-groups-are-unimodular]]). Then $L^2(\mathbb R)\ne\{0\}$ and $\lambda$ has no nonzero irreducible subrepresentation: every irreducible unitary representation of the abelian group $\mathbb R$ is one-dimensional ([[thm-schurs-lemma-for-unitary-representations]]), and a one-dimensional subrepresentation is spanned by a unit vector $v\in L^2(\mathbb R)$ with $\lambda(t)v=\chi(t)v$ for a continuous character $\chi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb T$; since $|\chi(t)|=1$, this gives $|v(x-t)|=|v(x)|$ for every $t$ and almost every $x$, so $v=0$ by [[lem-an-l-two-class-invariant-in-modulus-under-all-translations-of-the-line-is-zero]], contradicting $\|v\|=1$. Hence $\lambda$ is not a Hilbert direct sum of irreducible subrepresentations: in any such decomposition of a nonzero space at least one irreducible summand would be nonzero, and it would be an irreducible subrepresentation, which does not exist. Consequently the compact Peter-Weyl decomposition genuinely requires compactness, and the noncompact theory must use direct integrals: the Fourier-Plancherel transform realizes $\lambda$ as the direct integral $\int^\oplus_{\mathbb R}\chi_\xi\,d\xi$ of the characters, whose fibers are not square-integrable ([[def-hilbert-direct-sum-of-unitary-representations]] is used only for the direct-sum notion).
items.strategy: Assume a Hilbert direct sum decomposition into irreducibles exists and derive a contradiction by producing an irreducible subrepresentation, which the abelian/Schur argument reduces to a one-dimensional character eigenvector, and then forcing that eigenvector to vanish; the Fourier-Plancherel positive counterpart is stated as the source's direct-integral description and is not reproved here. The only analytic input is the local translation-invariance lemma, proved from the L1 approximate identity and the a.e.-subsequence theorem.
